reasoning.Student A: Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, truth-telling is a dominant strategy: no matter what others report, I cannot obtain a better outcome by misrepresenting my preferences. Although I have highest priority at w and y (w:1, y:1) and many applicants favor y > x > w > z, attempting to manipulate by ranking a safer school higher (e.g., putting w above y) cannot improve my assignment compared to submitting my true preferences. Therefore I should submit my sincere ordering y > x > w > z.
reasoning.Student B: Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, the dominant strategy is to report my true preferences — no misrepresentation can yield a better outcome regardless of what others do. My true order is z > y > x > w. Although many applicants favor y > x > w > z and I have top priority at x and z (priority 1) and lower priority at y and w (priority 2), that does not change the fact that truth-telling is optimal under a strategy-proof mechanism. Trying to list a safer option (e.g., x ahead of z) cannot improve my expected match compared to honestly listing z first.

reasoning.Student D: Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, I cannot get a better outcome by misrepresenting my preferences regardless of what others report. Although many applicants prefer y > x > w > z and my priorities at w and x are lower (w:4, x:4) than at y and z (y:3, z:3), that does not create an incentive to rank a less-preferred school higher: honesty is a dominant strategy.
